name: Davaka
rise: A small kingdom in the Kopili–Jamuna valley, named beside Kamarupa as a frontier state on Samudragupta's Allahabad pillar (c. 350–375).
fall: Absorbed into Kamarupa during the 5th century; the exact reign is not known.

name: Kamarupa: Varman dynasty
rise: Pushyavarman founds the first historical dynasty of Kamarupa around 350, with its capital at Pragjyotishpura (Guwahati).
fall: Bhaskaravarman, the greatest Varman king and friend of Harsha, dies c. 650 without an heir. The line ends with him (or with Avantivarman, c. 655).

name: Kamarupa: Mlechchha (Salastambha) dynasty
rise: Salastambha, a local chief, seizes the throne after the Varmans fail, c. 650. The capital later moves to Haruppeswara (Tezpur).
fall: Tyagasimha dies without an heir c. 900 and the nobles choose Brahmapala, beginning the Pala line.

name: Kamarupa: Pala dynasty
rise: Brahmapala is elected king c. 900. Ratnapala builds the fortified capital Durjaya.
fall: After Jayapala (c. 1100) the Pala line ends; Ramapala of Bengal takes the west and Kamarupa breaks into pieces.

name: Srihatta (Sylhet) kingdoms
rise: After Kamarupa's hold on the south lapses, Srihatta (Sylhet) is ruled by the Chandra kings of Harikela (10th–11th c.) and then by local Gaur kings.
fall: In 1303 Shah Jalal and the Bengal Sultanate defeat Gour Govinda, the last Gaur king.

name: Kamarupa successor polities
rise: Early 12th–mid 13th-century authority is known unevenly from grants, inscriptions and chronicles. The context polygon represents several successor powers; it is not one securely bounded unified kingdom.
fall: Sandhya is associated with reorganisation toward Kamata after 1257; the capital shift, often placed around 1260, is not exactly dated.

name: Pala Empire of Bengal
rise: Ramapala of Bengal conquers western Kamarupa c. 1110 and puts Timgyadeva in charge.
fall: Vaidyadeva’s appointment and later autonomy are reconstructed. Kamauli’s absolute date and the duration of Bengal’s control remain disputed.

name: Chutia kingdom
rise: Early foundation is uncertain. Birpal and 1187 are later traditions; the 1392 grant records Satyanarayana and the Sadiya genealogy of Nandin. Early map patches are symbolic.
fall: Independent kingship ends in the Ahom conquest of c.1523–1524; Chutia communities and traditions continue.

name: Ahom kingdom
rise: Sukaphaa enters the Assam plains by the Patkai corridor in 1228, moves between settlements and establishes the enduring capital at Charaideo in the conventional 1253 chronology.
fall: Civil war, the Moamoria rebellion and three Burmese invasions (1817–1821) destroy it. The British restore Purandar Singha in Upper Assam (1833) but annex it in 1838.

name: Kamata kingdom
rise: Kamata emerges through western reorganisation associated with Sandhya, conventionally c.1250–1270. The capital moves toward Kamatapur probably after 1257, often placed around 1260;1257 is the map’s display anchor.
fall: Bhuyan kings take the throne after Indranarayan; the last of them, Mriganka, gives way to the Khen c. 1440.

name: Dimasa (Kachari) kingdom
rise: The Dimasa rule the Dhansiri and Kopili valleys from Dimapur from the 13th century.
fall: Pushed from Dimapur (1536) to Maibong and then Khaspur, the kingdom is annexed by the British in 1832; Tularam's hill state lasts to 1854.

name: Bhuyan chiefs
rise: Separate landed chiefdoms and temporary alliances, not a unified dynasty or permanently twelve states. Charit traditions, Bardowa and regional records identify different lineages and seats.
fall: Koch and Ahom campaigns progressively subordinate regional chiefs in the early 16th century. Bhuyan families, offices and later resistance continue.

name: Khen kingdom of Kamata
rise: Niladhwaj founds the Khen dynasty at Kamatapur c. 1440. Nilambar extends it into Kamrup and Darrang.
fall: Alauddin Husain Shah of Bengal storms Kamatapur in 1498 and captures Nilambar.

name: Bengal Sultanate
rise: Bengal's sultans take Sylhet (1303) and, under Husain Shah, Kamata up to Hajo (1498).
fall: The Bhuyans drive out the Kamata garrison c. 1505; Sylhet passes to Afghan chiefs and then the Mughals.

name: Jaintia kingdom
rise: Founded c. 1500 in the Jaintia hills and the plains around Jaintiapur.
fall: Annexed by the British in 1835.

name: Koch kingdom
rise: From a small Chikna foothill chiefdom, Bisu/Biswa Singha built alliances and subdued neighbouring chiefs in stages. 1515 is the conventional start; kingship and capital-move dates differ between accounts.
fall: Under Nara Narayan the kingdom reaches its height; in 1581 it splits into Koch Bihar and Koch Hajo.

name: Koch Hajo
rise: Eastern Koch successor state from 1581. Its core is reconstructed between Sankosh and Barnadi within Assam, with eastern dependencies distinguished from core.
fall: The 1612–1613 Mughal invasion ends independent Koch Hajo; subsequent resistance and Ahom-protected Darrang are distinct outcomes.

name: Koch Khaspur (Cachar)
rise: A Koch line set up by Chilarai's campaigns rules the Cachar plains from Khaspur.
fall: Merges into the Dimasa kingdom c. 1745 by marriage.

name: Mughal Empire
rise: Rajmahal (1576) begins the imperial Bengal phase; eastern consolidation follows in 1611–1612, Koch Hajo in 1612–1613, and Chittagong in 1666. These are separate campaigns.
fall: Defeated at Saraighat (1671) and finally at Itakhuli (1682); the Manas becomes the frontier. The Bengal Diwani passes to the East India Company in 1765.

name: Matak territory (Bengmara)
rise: After the Moamoria rebellion, the Matak leader Sarbananda Singha is recognised as Barsenapati of an autonomous territory (1805).
fall: Annexed by the British in 1839.

name: Burmese (Konbaung) occupation
rise: Invited in by rival nobles, Burmese armies invade in 1817 and 1819 and occupy the whole valley from 1821.
fall: Driven out by the British in the First Anglo-Burmese War (1824–1826); Assam is ceded by the Treaty of Yandabo (1826).

name: British India
rise: The East India Company holds Goalpara and Sylhet from 1765 (Bengal Diwani) and takes all of Assam after the First Anglo-Burmese War (1826).
fall: India becomes independent on 15 August 1947; Sylhet goes to Pakistan after a referendum.

name: Assam (independent India)
rise: Assam becomes a province and then (1950) a state of independent India, still covering most of the north-east.
fall: Nagaland (1963), Meghalaya, Mizoram and Arunachal (1972) are carved out; the present state dates from 1972.

name: East Pakistan (Sylhet)
rise: Sylhet votes to join Pakistan in the 1947 referendum; Karimganj stays in India.
fall: Becomes part of Bangladesh in 1971.

name: Bangladesh (Sylhet)
rise: Bangladesh becomes independent in 1971.

name: States carved out of Assam
rise: Nagaland (1963), Meghalaya, Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh (1972) are separated from Assam.
